options.label: A
options.text: Formation of amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix

options.label: C
options.text: Formation of blebs in the plasma membrane

options.label: D
options.text: Detachment of ribosomes from the granular endoplasmic reticulum

questions.answerText: Formation of amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix
questions.solutionHtml:
p> 

Explanation:

 

Formation of amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix is typically associated with irreversible cell injury rather than reversible cell injury. This change indicates severe damage to the mitochondria, often due to sustained injury that compromises mitochondrial function beyond the cell's ability to recover.

 

Other Options Explained:

 

Option B. Diminished generation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP): This is characteristic of reversible cell injury. It occurs due to temporary impairment of mitochondrial function, which can recover if the injurious stimulus is removed.

 

Option C. Formation of blebs in the plasma membrane: Blebbing is a response to reversible cell injury. It involves changes in the cytoskeleton and plasma membrane, which can be restored once the injury ceases.

 

Option D. Detachment of ribosomes from the granular endoplasmic reticulum: This change can occur during reversible cell injury and reflects a temporary disruption in protein synthesis. If the injury is mild and transient, normal ribosomal function can resume.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Amorphous densities in mitochondria are a hallmark of irreversible injury, while diminished ATP production, membrane blebbing, and ribosome detachment are associated with reversible cell injury

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary consequence of diminished ATP on cellular function?
questions.solutionHtml:
dysfunction. This exaggerates release of lysosomal enzymes and membrane damage.

 

Explanation:

Option A. Diminished ATP can actually lead to an increase in intracellular calcium as ATP-dependent mechanisms that pump calcium out of the cell fail. An increase in intracellular calcium can activate destructive enzymes and pathways.

 

Option C. Diminished ATP typically leads to damage of cellular membranes because energy-dependent ion pumps and repair mechanisms fail, rather than preserving membrane integrity.

 

Option D. A decrease in ATP can contribute to the release of lysosomal enzymes. When ATP is low, cellular components may not be maintained or recycled properly, leading to enzyme leakage and further cellular damage.

 

Educational Objective:

Diminished ATP most directly leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, as the mitochondria are the main site of ATP production within the cell. This mitochondrial dysfunction can subsequently lead to additional cellular damage, including the release of lysosomal enzymes and membrane damage.

Option B. Decreased anaerobic glycolysis: Anaerobic glycolysis actually increases in response to hypoxia as the cell attempts to compensate for the lack of oxygen and maintain ATP production.

 

Option C. Decreased production of 2,3 DPG from alternative glycolytic pathway: This is not the primary mechanism of hypoxic cell injury. While changes in 2,3-DPG levels affect oxygen release from hemoglobin, they do not directly cause cellular injury.

The primary mechanism of hypoxic cell injury is decreased aerobic oxidative respiration which directly results in diminished ATP production and consequent cellular dysfunction.

questions.answerText: Thought to be derived from damaged cellular membranes
questions.solutionHtml:
as of cellular membrane damage.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Myelin figures are composed of phospholipids, not triglycerides.

 

Option B and Option C. Myelin figures can be observed in both reversible and irreversible cell injury scenarios.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Myelin figures, which may be seen in renal biopsies from patients with drug-induced nephrotoxicity, are derived from damaged cellular membranes and can be indicative of both reversible and irreversible cell injury.

 

 

Why myelin figures are seen in both reversible and irreversible cell injury? 

 

Reversible injury (early stage):

 

  • In mild/moderate injury, damage to membranes starts.
  • The injured membranes can form small amounts of myelin figures.
  • At this point, the cell may still recover if the stress is removed.
  • Typical associated changes: cell swelling (hydropic change), dilation of ER, ribosome detachment.

 

So, few or small myelin figures can be seen during reversible injury as the cell responds to stress.

 

Irreversible injury (severe stage):

 

  • When damage becomes severe and progressive → massive membrane breakdown.
  • The number and size of myelin figures increase markedly.
  • They can become large, prominent, and sometimes are phagocytosed by macrophages or degraded into fatty acids → leading to calcium deposits (calcification).

 

So, in irreversible injury, abundant myelin figures reflect extensive, fatal membrane damage.

Reason (R): There may be loss of nuclear material in irreversible cell injury

options.label: B

questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="text-align:justify;">Option B:

 

Assertion (A):

 

Necrotic cells have a glassy, homogeneous appearance when compared to normal cells in irreversible cell injury.

 

  • True
  • In irreversible injury → necrosis:
    • Cytoplasm appears more eosinophilic (pink)
    • Glassy, homogeneous look
  • This happens because:
    • Loss of glycogen particles
    • Protein denaturation
    • Loss of cell detail → makes cytoplasm look smooth and glassy

 

Reason (R):

 

There may be loss of nuclear material in irreversible cell injury

 

  • True
  • In necrosis, nuclei undergo:
    • Pyknosis (shrinkage, dark)
    • Karyorrhexis (fragmentation)
    • Karyolysis (fading, loss)
  • So yes, there is loss of nuclear material.
  • The glassy, homogeneous cytoplasmic appearance is mainly due to:
    • Loss of glycogen
    • Denaturation and aggregation of cytoplasmic proteins
  • The loss of nuclear material does happen in necrosis, but it does not explain the glassy appearance of the cytoplasm.
  • Nuclear changes and cytoplasmic changes are parallel but separate processes.

 

The necrotic cell may have a glassy homogeneous appearance relative to normal cells, mainly as a result of the loss of glycogen particles. When enzymes have digested the cell’s organelles, the cytoplasm becomes vacuolated and appears moth-eaten.

 

However, loss of nuclear material is also a characteristic finding in irreversible cellular injury.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Necrotic cells can exhibit a glassy, homogeneous appearance due to the loss of intracellular components like glycogen, while the loss of nuclear material is also a characteristic of irreversible cell injury, but it is not the explanation for the glassy appearance.

questions.stem: Physiological hyperplasia and hypertrophy are seen simultaneously in? Uterus in pregnancy Skeletal muscle in athletes Breast at puberty Left ventricle of heart in hypertensive patients
questions.solutionHtml:
w Roman",serif">Ans. C) Both 1 and 3

 

Explanation:

 

Option 1: During pregnancy, the uterus undergoes both hyperplasia (increased number of cells) and hypertrophy (increase in the size of existing cells) as a physiological response to accommodate and support the developing fetus. This dual increase in size and number of cells allows the uterus to significantly expand during pregnancy.

 

Option 2:  Athletes who undergo rigorous training often experience skeletal muscle hypertrophy, which is the increase in the size of muscle cells, but not typically hyperplasia, which would be an increase in the number of muscle cells. Muscle growth in athletes is usually attributed to hypertrophy from repetitive use and strain.

 

Option 3: During puberty, the female breast displays both hyperplasia, with the proliferation of glandular epithelium, and hypertrophy, with the enlargement of the glandular epithelial cells. This dual change is stimulated by hormonal influences and is a natural part of sexual maturation.

 

Option 4: In hypertensive patients, the left ventricle may undergo hypertrophy due to increased resistance that the heart has to pump against. This is not a physiological but rather a pathological response and typically does not involve hyperplasia, which would be characterized by an increased number of cardiac muscle cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the uterus during pregnancy and the breast at puberty, physiological changes involve both hyperplasia (increase in the number of cells) and hypertrophy (increase in the size of cells). These changes are driven by hormonal influences that are part of natural growth and development processes.

g>Ans. C) 1, 2, 3, 4

Anaplasia: This refers to a lack of differentiation within cells and is characteristic of malignant tumors, where cells lose the morphological features of mature cells and their organization. Anaplastic cells often show variations in size and shape, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and prominent nucleoli.

 

Option 2. Metaplasia: This is a process whereby one differentiated cell type is replaced by another cell type, which can occur due to chronic irritation or inflammation. While metaplasia is not cancer, it can sometimes progress to dysplasia and then to cancer.

Anaplasia, metaplasia, hamartoma and dysplasia are conditions with cells that have an increased risk of malignancy.

Option C. It is not associated with architectural abnormalities: This statement is false. Dysplasia is often associated with a loss of normal tissue architecture, including the uniformity and architectural orientation of cells.

Mesenchymal cells can undergo changes that may be equivalent to dysplasia, such as in fibroblastic proliferations, but the term dysplasia is usually used with epithelial pathology.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dysplasia is characterized by cellular pleomorphism, which refers to variations in size and shape among cells, commonly observed in epithelial tissues where disordered growth is present.

questions.stem: Given the importance of lifestyle factors in the modulation of lifespan, which of the following interventions is most reliably associated with an extension of longevity?

options.label: A
options.text: Regular exercise like walking for 30 minutes

questions.solutionHtml:
Option A. Regular exercise like walking for 30 minutes: Regular physical activity is widely recognized for its benefits in improving health and quality of life, but it has not been definitively shown to extend lifespan.

 

Option B. Reducing stress:  can have numerous health benefits and can improve quality of life, but its direct impact on extending lifespan is complex and not as well-established as other interventions.

 

Option D. Increasing food intake:  does not contribute to lifespan extension and, without proper balance, can lead to obesity and associated health problems that may shorten life expectancy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The most reliable intervention for extending lifespan, as indicated by extensive research, is reducing caloric intake by approximately 30%. This strategy decreases the nutrient-mediated release of growth factors that have been implicated in accelerating the aging process and increasing mortality.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement about senescence?

options.label: A
options.text: Aging is associated with decreased telomerase activity

options.label: B
options.text: Aging is associated with increased telomerase activity

options.label: C
options.text: Stem cells have reduced telomerase activity

questions.answerText: Aging is associated with decreased telomerase activity
questions.solutionHtml:
n:justify;">Explanation:

 

Option B. Aging is associated with increased telomerase activity: This is generally incorrect for normal somatic cells, as aging does not typically come with increased telomerase activity, which is often associated with immortalized cancer cells.

 

Option C. Stem cells have reduced telomerase activity: This statement is generally not true; stem cells and germ cells often have higher levels of telomerase activity, allowing them to maintain telomere length and proliferative capacity.

 

Option D. Associated with increased cell replication: Senescence is actually associated with a decrease or cessation in cell replication due to telomere shortening and the activation of tumor suppressor genes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Aging in somatic cells is associated with decreased telomerase activity, which contributes to telomere shortening and the subsequent arrest of cell division, a process known as replicative senescence.

 

Telomerase:

 

  • Telomerase is an enzyme (a type of reverse transcriptase) that adds telomeric repeats to the ends of chromosomes.
  • Normal somatic cells:
    • Have very low or absent telomerase activity.
    • With each cell division, telomeres progressively shorten.
    • When they get too short → cells enter replicative senescence and stop dividing.
  • Stem cells and germ cells:
    • Have higher telomerase activity → helps maintain telomere length and allows many more divisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the etiology of Werner syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml:
ont-family:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Telomerase lengthening is typically related to cellular mechanisms that allow for unlimited replication, as seen in cancer cells, not premature aging.

 

Option B. Mutations in the lamin proteins are related to various disorders, including some forms of premature aging, but not specifically Werner syndrome.

 

Option C. While lipid peroxidation can contribute to cellular damage and aging, it is not the genetic etiology of Werner syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The genetic etiology of Werner syndrome is a defect in DNA helicase leading to premature aging due to the inability to properly replicate and repair DNA, which results in accelerated chromosomal damage.

Dysplasia represents an early sign of potential malignant transformation in cervical epithelial cells and is characterized by disorganized cellular architecture and nuclear atypia.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man goes on a fun trip to Goa and spends 6 hours on the beach in day time. The next day he has a darker complexion. His skin does not show warmth, erythema, or tenderness. His skin tone fades to its original appearance within a month. Which of the following substances contributes the most to the biochemical process leading to these skin changes?

Option A. Heme containing iron as part of hemosiderin from breakdown of red blood cells can impart a brownish colour, but this is typically local from trauma or more global as part of an iron storage disease such as hemochromatosis. Iron oxide is also used in tattoo pigments.

 

Option C. Homogentisic acid can be part of the process of the rare disease alkaptonuria, in which a black pigment is deposited in connective tissues

questions.stem: The lifestyle patterns of healthy persons from 20 to 30 years of age are studied. A subset of these persons has a lifestyle characterized by consumption of a lot of pizza and very little physical exercise. Which of the following tissue changes is most likely to develop in this subset of persons as a consequence of this lifestyle?

options.label: D

Explanation:

 

Option A. Fatty change in the liver is due to toxic and metabolic derangements, such as those that occur with malnutrition or alcoholism.  Similarly, fatty change in the heart (Option B) is a consequence of toxic or hypoxic events.

 

Option D. Muscle does not typically undergo metaplasia in response to weight gain. Adipocytes in fascial planes and around the muscle can increase in size. The muscle may atrophy in response to the sedentary lifestyle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In adults, hypertrophy of adipocytes, or steatocytes, is the primary tissue change associated with weight gain due to excessive caloric intake and insufficient exercise, as this leads to an increase in fat cell size.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman Yashi gives birth to her first child. She begins breast feeding the infant. She continues breast feeding for almost 6 months with no difficulties and no complications. Which of the following cellular processes that began in the breast during pregnancy allowed her to nurse the infant for this period of time?
questions.solutionHtml:
y progesterone with pregnancy, to provide for lactation.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Metaplasia is the exchange of the normal epithelium for another in response to chronic irritation.

 

Option B. The stroma of the breast consists of connective tissue that provides structural support, but does not have cells that produce milk.

 

Option C. Dysplasia in epithelia is a pre-malignant change not part of normal physiologic events. This would be a precursor to breast cancer. Pregnancy is a protective factor against breast cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lobular hyperplasia that is particularly influenced by progesterone, facilitates lactation postpartum.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with a painful and tender nodule on her shin. She reports a history of tuberculosis and was treated successfully. A biopsy of the lesion shows a granulomatous inflammation with giant cells. What type of giant cells is most likely present in her lesion?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option B. Foreign body giant cells arise when foreign materials, too large to be phagocytosed by a single macrophage, are present in the tissue. Their nuclei are haphazardly arranged within the cell, and these cells are often associated with chronic inflammation due to persistent foreign bodies.

 

Option C. Touton giant cells are typically found in fat necrosis and some tumors. They have a ring of nuclei surrounded by foamy cytoplasm and are not typically associated with granulomatous inflammation from tuberculosis.

 

Option D. Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells are multinucleated giant cells found in the hyperplastic lymphoid tissue, commonly associated with measles and other viral infections, not tuberculosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient with a history of tuberculosis, Langhans giant cells are indicative of a granulomatous response to mycobacterial antigens. These cells are formed from the fusion of macrophages and are characteristic of the granulomas seen in tuberculosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a painless mass on her thigh. She reports a history of trauma to the area several years ago. Imaging studies show a well-defined mass with calcifications. A biopsy of the lesion shows a granulomatous inflammation with giant cells. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for the development of granulomatous inflammation in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A. Chronic smoking can cause a variety of pulmonary problems and has been associated with an increased risk of developing granulomas in the lungs. However, it is less likely to cause a localized granulomatous reaction in the soft tissue of the thigh as a response to an old injury.

 

Option B. Immune dysregulation can lead to granulomatous diseases like sarcoidosis, where the immune system creates granulomas in various organs without a known foreign body or pathogen. This systemic process usually doesn't result in an isolated thigh mass related to a previous trauma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the setting of a prior trauma with subsequent development of a mass, the biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is most consistent with a foreign body reaction.

questions.stem: The cells seen after 72 hours in the infarcted area in MI are:
questions.solutionHtml:
>Option A: Neutrophils are the first inflammatory cells to infiltrate the area of myocardial necrosis, peaking at about 1-3 days post-MI. However, by 72 hours, their numbers are diminishing as they are replaced by other inflammatory cells.

 

Option B: Lymphocytes are part of the adaptive immune response and are not the predominant cell type at 72 hours post-MI.

 

Option D: Monocytes are the precursors to macrophages. They circulate in the bloodstream and migrate to the site of infarction, where they differentiate into macrophages. By 72 hours, these cells would have already become macrophages within the tissue.

 

Educational Objective:

 

At 72 hours following a myocardial infarction, macrophages are the predominant cells in the infarcted area, playing a critical role in debris clearance and initiating the reparative processes.

In TTC staining during autopsy, viable myocardium is indicated by a brick-red color, which results from the presence of active dehydrogenase enzymes that reduce the TTC dye.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man suffered a massive cardiac arrest and encountered sudden death. Post mortem finding of the heart shows complete obstruction of left anterior descending artery by an atherosclerotic plaque. Which type of necrosis will be identified in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
g ischemia, as would occur with an obstructed coronary artery.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B. Fibrinoid necrosis is usually associated with immune reactions in blood vessels, as seen in conditions like vasculitis, not with ischemic heart disease.

 

Option C. This type of necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis infections, where affected tissues display a cheese-like appearance, not typically associated with myocardial infarction.

 

Option D. Gangrenous necrosis is a term used more commonly in the clinical setting to describe limb death due to severe ischemia, and although it can involve coagulative necrosis, it's not the specific type seen with a blocked coronary artery in the heart.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the event of a massive cardiac arrest with an obstructed left anterior descending artery, the type of necrosis expected in the heart is coagulative necrosis, which is characterized by the preservation of the basic outline of the cells after cell death due to ischemia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a 30-year history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. He has had extensive black discoloration of skin and soft tissue of his right foot, with areas of yellowish exudate, for the past 2 months. Staphylococcus aureus is cultured from this exudate. A below-the-knee amputation is performed. The amputation specimen received in the surgical pathology laboratory is most likely to demonstrate which of the following pathologic abnormalities?
questions.solutionHtml:
g>

 

Option A. A neoplasm is a mass lesion.

 

Option C. Vasculitis (with either thrombosis or hemorrhage), would be more likely manifested throughout the body. Coagulopathy is not a feature of diabetes mellitus.

 

Option D. Caseation is a part of granulomatous inflammation. Caseating granulomas are soft, cheesy, and white.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gangrene, particularly wet gangrene is characterized by black discoloration and exudate in a diabetic patient, and is a consequence of coagulative necrosis coupled with bacterial infection, typically necessitating amputation of the affected area.

questions.stem: As a baby develops in utero, fingers and toes are attached together in the form of webs. Around 10 weeks of gestation, fingers and toes separate, elongate and lose their webbing. Which of the following physiological processes aids this?
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>

 

Option A. Free radical injury is typically harmful and not a normal part of physiological development.

 

Option B. This is a form of programmed cell death, but it is not responsible for the normal differentiation and development processes that occur in utero.

 

Option C. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of non-apoptotic cell death, not involved in the typical development of fingers and toes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Apoptosis plays a key role in embryonic development, including the separation and elongation of fingers and toes, by removing excess cells to shape the developing tissues correctly.

:12pt">Option A. Annexin A1, not annexin V, is associated with hairy cell leukemia.

Explanation:

questions.stem: An elderly patient dies due to a cancer and his cells in the cancer affected area were examined. Ultra structurally, the most prominent features found are the loss of mitochondrial cristae and ruptured outer mitochondrial membrane. Which of the following best can be the pattern of cell death here?
questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="text-align:justify">Ferroptosis is a form of regulated cell death caused by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, leading to loss of mitochondrial cristae and rupture of the outer mitochondrial membrane.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Necrosis is a form of cell death characterized by uncontrolled cell lysis, often resulting in inflammation.

 

Option B. Necroptosis is a type of programmed necrosis that is dependent on receptor-interacting protein kinases and often associated with inflammation.

 

Option D. Pyroptosis is an inflammatory form of programmed cell death associated with the activation of caspase-1 and often seen in immune cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death pathway marked by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, resulting in distinctive ultrastructural changes such as loss of mitochondrial cristae and rupture of the outer mitochondrial membrane, commonly associated with cancer, neurodegeneration, and stroke.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a form of programmed cell death that is dependent on the formation of autophagosomes and leads to the degradation of cellular components?
questions.solutionHtml:
serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Necroptosis is a form of programmed cell death that resembles necrosis, characterized by cell swelling and membrane rupture, typically involving death receptors like TNFR1 but is not associated with autophagosomes.

 

Option B. Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death involving cell shrinkage, DNA fragmentation, and the formation of apoptotic bodies, without the formation of autophagosomes.

 

Option C. Pyroptosis is an inflammatory form of programmed cell death that occurs upon activation of inflammasomes and leads to cell lysis and inflammation, not primarily involving autophagosomes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Autophagy is a form of programmed cell death characterized by the formation of autophagosomes that engulf and degrade cellular components in response to cellular stress.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents with fatigue, weakness, and pallor. Laboratory investigations reveal a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Peripheral blood smear shows microcytic red blood cells, and bone marrow biopsy confirms the presence of ringed sideroblasts. The patient does not have a history of significant alcohol consumption. Which of the following treatments is most likely to improve the anemia in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
family:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

Option A. iron supplementation is used for iron deficiency anemia, which typically does not feature ringed sideroblasts. In sideroblastic anemia, there is usually adequate or increased iron in the body, but it's not properly incorporated into hemoglobin.

Option B.Thiamine deficiency does not typically cause sideroblastic anemia, so supplementation would not address the underlying pathophysiology in this case.

Option D. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, not typically sideroblastic anemia, so this would not be the treatment of choice for a patient with ringed sideroblasts.

Educational Objective:

Sideroblastic anemia can be responsive to pyridoxine supplementation, especially when ringed sideroblasts are observed on bone marrow biopsy and the patient does not have a history of conditions that could cause secondary sideroblastic anemia, such as alcoholism or lead poisoning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a form of programmed cell death that is dependent on caspase-1 and leads to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18?
questions.solutionHtml:
with the release of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18, often in response to infection.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Necrosis is a form of cell death that occurs due to injury or disease and is characterized by the uncontrolled release of cellular contents, not typically associated with a caspase-dependent mechanism.

 

Option B. Although apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death, it is primarily associated with caspase-3 and caspase-9 and does not typically result in an inflammatory response.

 

Option D. Autophagy is a process of cellular "self-eating" that recycles cellular components and does not directly lead to cell death or the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pyroptosis is a type of programmed cell death that is dependent on caspase-1 activation and results in the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18. It is initiated in response to infection by intracellular pathogens and can be triggered by the activation of pattern recognition receptors such as NOD-like receptors.

questions.stem: Which caspase is not typically involved in the process of pyroptosis, a form of cell death associated with microbial infection and inflammatory response?
questions.solutionHtml:
="text-align:justify">Option A. Caspase 1 is a central enzyme in the pyroptotic pathway, responsible for the cleavage of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β and initiating the pyroptotic cell death.

 

Option C. Caspase 4 is implicated in the detection of bacterial endotoxins and can initiate noncanonical pyroptosis upon sensing these intracellular signals.

A chest x-ray shows evidence of pneumonia, and he is started on antibiotics. Despite treatment, his condition deteriorates, and a bronchoalveolar lavage is performed, which reveals the presence of cells undergoing a type of cell death characterized by swelling, membrane rupture, and the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). t-size:12pt">Explanation:

Option A: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death involving cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, and DNA fragmentation, without inflammation or DAMP release.

 

Option B: Pyroptosis is a form of inflammatory programmed cell death associated with infection and is characterized by the activation of inflammatory caspases, cell swelling, membrane pore formation, and release of inflammatory cytokines.

 

Option C: Autophagy is a process where cells degrade their own components through the lysosomal machinery, typically as a survival mechanism in response to stress, without immediate cell death or DAMP release.

 

Educational Objective:

Necroptosis is a form of programmed cell death marked by cellular swelling, membrane disruption, and DAMP release, which can be associated with conditions such as COPD and infection-related inflammation.

Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) is an antioxidant enzyme that protects cells from the damaging effects of superoxide radicals (O2•−) by catalyzing their conversion to oxygen (O2) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). It is crucial in modulating ROS levels and preventing cellular damage, but it does not directly generate free radicals for bacterial killing.

 

Option B. The Fenton reaction describes the iron-catalyzed conversion of hydrogen peroxide into hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are highly reactive and can cause significant damage to cellular components. This reaction can contribute to the bactericidal activity of phagocytes following engulfment of pathogens.

Explanation:

 

Option A. Catalase is an enzyme found in nearly all living organisms exposed to oxygen. It catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, thereby protecting the cell from oxidative damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS). Thus, it acts as an antioxidant.

 

Option B. Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) is an enzyme that protects the cell against harmful effects of superoxide radicals by catalyzing their conversion into less harmful molecules, oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. It is indeed an antioxidant enzyme.

 

Option D. Transferrin is a glycoprotein that binds iron ions and transports them to different parts of the body. Iron-free transferrin, also known as apotransferrin, can bind free iron and, by doing so, limits iron-induced oxidative stress since free iron can catalyze the formation of harmful free radicals. Therefore, it has antioxidant properties.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Unlike the other options listed, phagocyte oxidase is not an antioxidant. Instead, it generates reactive oxygen species as part of the immune response to destroy pathogens.

 

Antioxidants:

 

  • Substances that neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and free radicals, preventing cell injury.
  • Major enzymatic antioxidants:
    • Catalase: breaks down H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂
    • Superoxide dismutase (SOD): converts superoxide (O₂•–) → H₂O₂
    • Glutathione peroxidase: reduces H₂O₂ and organic peroxides
  • Non-enzymatic antioxidants: vitamins A,C,E.
  • Transferrin, ferritin, ceruloplasmin: bind free iron or copper → reduce ROS generation via Fenton reaction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old ingests a large amount of paracetamol and 12 hours later develops malaise and abdominal pain. Laboratory studies show an elevated ALT. N-acetylcysteine is administered to aid in generation of which of the following enzymes within cells as a protective mechanism to reduce the number of free radicals?
questions.solutionHtml:
ext-align:justify"> 

Option B. Catalase is an enzyme found in the peroxisomes of cells that decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. It does not directly use substrates provided by N-acetylcysteine for its action.

 

Option C. Hydrogen peroxide is not an enzyme; rather, it is a reactive oxygen species that is decomposed by enzymes such as catalase and glutathione peroxidase.

 

Option D. NADPH oxidase is an enzyme complex found in phagocytes that generates reactive oxygen species, such as hydrogen peroxide, used for the killing of pathogens. It is not involved in the detoxification of free radicals related to paracetamol toxicity.

N-acetylcysteine aids in the synthesis of glutathione, thereby enhancing the activity of glutathione peroxidase to reduce the oxidative stress caused by a paracetamol overdose.

This stain is used to detect iron deposits in tissues and is characteristic of the pathology seen in hemochromatosis, where iron accumulation occurs within the hepatocytes.

options.label: A
options.text: It may be caused by multiple myeloma

options.label: D
options.text: Calcium deposition occurs in dead tissues

questions.answerText: Calcium deposition occurs in dead tissues
questions.solutionHtml:

Explanation:

 

Option A. It may be caused by multiple myeloma: Multiple myeloma itself does not cause dystrophic calcification. However, it can lead to systemic changes that result in pathologic calcifications. Dystrophic calcification is specifically associated with local tissue damage and necrosis, not directly with plasma cell disorders like multiple myeloma.

 

Option B. It never causes organ dysfunction: This statement is incorrect. While dystrophic calcification occurs in non-viable tissues, it can interfere with organ function depending on the size and location of the calcifications.

 

Option C. It is associated with hypercalcaemia: Dystrophic calcification can occur despite normal serum levels of calcium. It is not typically associated with hypercalcemia, which is more commonly linked with metastatic calcification.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dystrophic calcification is the deposition of calcium salts in non-viable or dying tissues and can occur with normal serum calcium levels, often leading to organ dysfunction if extensive.

 

Dystrophic calcification:

 

  • Calcium deposits in dead, dying, or damaged tissues.
  • Occurs despite normal serum calcium and phosphate levels.
  • Typical sites:
    • Old scars
    • Atherosclerotic plaques
    • Areas of caseous necrosis (e.g., TB)
    • Aging or damaged heart valves

 

 

Ref: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of disease 10th ed PG: 59

Explanation:

 

Option A. Atherosclerotic vessels: These typically exhibit dystrophic calcification rather than metastatic. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or necrotic tissues and does not necessarily involve a systemic mineral imbalance.

 

Option C. Damaged heart valves: Damaged heart valves are more prone to dystrophic calcification because of the local tissue damage, rather than metastatic calcification which occurs in normal tissues.

 

Option D. Tuberculous lymph nodes: Tuberculous lymph nodes would typically have dystrophic calcification due to the localized damage caused by the infection rather than metastatic calcification which is usually related to an abnormal systemic calcium or phosphorus metabolism.

Metastatic calcification preferably occurs in normal tissues, like the gastric mucosa, when there is an elevated serum calcium level due to conditions such as hyperparathyroidism, bone destruction, vitamin D disorders, or renal failure.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presented sudden onset hemiplegia. Serial investigations were performed. She was diagnosed with psammomatous meningioma, a subtype of meningioma with several psammoma bodies. Similar type of calcification can be seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
on:

 

Option A. Milk alkali syndrome:  This condition is associated with hypercalcemia and not typically with dystrophic calcification. It results from excessive intake of calcium and absorbable alkali, leading to a constellation of symptoms including renal failure, metabolic alkalosis, and high levels of calcium in the blood.

 

Option C. Hyperparathyroidism: Hyperparathyroidism leads to hypercalcemia and can result in metastatic calcification, which occurs in normal tissues, not specifically in areas of necrosis or degeneration like dystrophic calcification.

 

Option D. Vitamin A intoxication:  While vitamin A intoxication can lead to a wide range of systemic effects, it is not directly linked with dystrophic calcification, which is localized to areas of tissue damage or necrosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dystrophic calcification is a type of pathological calcification that occurs in dead, dying, or degenerated tissue, where calcium metabolism is typically normal, and serum calcium levels are unchanged. This type of calcification can be observed in atheromatous plaques as well as in psammomatous meningiomas.

 

Psammoma bodies:

 

  • Psammoma bodies are round, concentric, laminated calcific structures.
  • They form by dystrophic calcification:
    • Deposition of calcium in degenerating, dead, or dying cells/tissue.
    • Serum calcium is normal.
  • Characteristically seen in:
    • Psammomatous meningioma
    • Papillary carcinoma of thyroid
    • Papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary
    • Sometimes mesothelioma and other papillary tumors.

questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic patient presented with increasing abdominal girth and decreased liver span. Liver biopsy features hepatocytes with reddish inclusions. What is in the content of the inclusions?
questions.solutionHtml:
iquitinylated keratins 8 and 18. These proteins form a dense network of filaments within the hepatocytes.

 

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Actin: Actin is a component of the cytoskeleton involved in various types of cell motility but is not the primary component of the reddish inclusions found in hepatocytes, which are characteristic of Mallory-Denk bodies.

 

Option C. Microtubules: Microtubules are part of the cytoskeleton and are involved in maintaining cell shape and intracellular transport but are not the substance that composes the reddish inclusions seen in this patient's liver biopsy.

 

Option D. Fibronectin is an extracellular matrix protein that plays a critical role in wound healing and cell adhesion. It is not typically found within hepatocyte inclusions like Mallory-Denk bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The reddish inclusions found within hepatocytes on a liver biopsy of a chronic alcoholic patient are composed of intermediate filaments, specifically ubiquitinated keratins 8 and 18, characteristic of Mallory-Denk bodies.

Explanation:

 

Option B. Golgi apparatus: This is an organelle involved in the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins, but it does not have the granular appearance shown in the image.

 

Option C. Secondary lysosomes: These are the organelles where digestion of macromolecules occurs. Secondary lysosomes can contain a variety of digested material, but they do not match the specific appearance of the structures shown.

Lipofuscin granules are identified in electron microscopy by their characteristic granular appearance, perinuclear position, and intralysosomal location, which align with the structures in the image.

 

Lipofuscin granules (also called residual bodies)

 

  • Origin: Lipofuscin is an autofluorescent pigment derived from lipid peroxidation of subcellular membranes; it accumulates in lysosomes as a product of incomplete degradation.
  • Appearance on EM:
    • Irregular in shape, not perfectly round.
    • Electron-dense (dark) with a heterogeneous internal structure.
    • May show whorled lamellar or granular material.
    • Often clustered near the nucleus (perinuclear).
  • Clinical context:
    • Common in long-lived cells (e.g., neurons, cardiac myocytes, hepatocytes).
    • Called “wear-and-tear” pigment because it accumulates with age.
  • Key point:
    • Because lipofuscin is undegradable material, it remains as residual bodies in the cell cytoplasm, separate from active digestion.
